summary: Explains why the Stringprep approach, used by IDNA2003 and several protocol profiles, needs revision, and states the problem for a new framework called PRECIS for preparing and comparing internationalized strings. It is a problem statement, and it is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Stringprep is the older way of preparing non-ASCII text so that protocols can compare it. It froze the set of allowed characters at Unicode 3.2 and never moved. This RFC sets out why that is a problem and what any replacement has to do about it.

subtitle: Why the old way of preparing internationalized text needs replacing, and what a replacement has to get right.

tldr.problem: Stringprep, the mechanism IETF protocols use to prepare and compare internationalized strings, is frozen at Unicode 3.2 and every protocol has invented its own profile on top of it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists what the protocols using Stringprep actually need, groups identifiers by how they can be compared, and then works through the character questions a replacement must answer: case, normalization, prohibited characters, delimiters and look-alike glyphs.
tldr.outcome: It is a problem statement, and it asks for a replacement framework to be defined along the lines of IDNA2008, with rules derived from Unicode properties rather than from a fixed list.

today: RFC 6885 is an Informational document, and the metadata shows no obsoleting and no updating RFC. It is the problem statement for the PRECIS framework, and it deliberately does not define a protocol; the framework itself was specified later by the PRECIS working group.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Internationalizing Domain Names in Applications, called IDNA2003, describes a mechanism for encoding Unicode labels that make up Internationalized Domain Names as standard DNS labels. The labels were processed using a method called Nameprep and Punycode. That method was specific to IDNA2003 but was generalized as Stringprep, a framework within which protocols define their Stringprep profiles.

Many IETF specifications use Stringprep, including the Nameprep profile for Internationalized Domain Names, the Inter-Asterisk eXchange protocol, NFSv4, the iSCSI profile for iSCSI names, the Extensible Authentication Protocol, the Nodeprep and Resourceprep profiles for XMPP, the IRI and URI profiles in XMPP, the Policy MIB profile for SNMP, TLS, the LDAP profile, LDAPprep for PKIX subject identification and for PKIX certificate revocation lists, the SASLprep profile used by SASL and by several SASL mechanisms, the trace profile for the SASL ANONYMOUS mechanism, and the Unicode casemap Unicode collation.

A review of these specifications found that they are very similar and can be grouped into a short number of classes, and many reuse the same Stringprep profile, such as the SASL one.

IDNA2003 was replaced because of limitations described in RFC 4690. The new specification, IDNA2008, was designed based on the considerations in RFC 5894. One of the effects of IDNA2008 is that Nameprep and Stringprep are not used at all. Instead, an algorithm based on Unicode properties of code points is defined. That algorithm generates a stable and complete table of the supported Unicode code points for each Unicode version, and it uses an inclusion-based approach instead of the exclusion-based approach of Stringprep and Nameprep. IDNA2003 created an explicit list of excluded or mapped-away characters, so anything in Unicode 3.2 that was not so listed could be assumed to be allowed under the protocol. IDNA2008 begins instead from the assumption that code points are disallowed and then relies on Unicode properties to derive whether a given code point actually is allowed in the protocol.

This document lists the shortcomings and issues found by the protocols listed above that defined Stringprep profiles, and it lists the requirements for any potential replacement of Stringprep. It defines the keyword PRECIS as Preparation and Comparison of Internationalized Strings.
sections.plainLanguage: Stringprep is the older way of preparing non-ASCII text so that protocols can compare it. It froze the set of allowed characters at Unicode 3.2 and never moved. This RFC sets out why that is a problem and what any replacement has to do about it.

sections.title: Why Stringprep Needed Replacing
sections.content:
During IETF 77 in March 2010, a Birds of a Feather discussed the current state of the protocols that had defined Stringprep profiles. The main conclusions were as follows.

Stringprep is bound to Version 3.2 of Unicode and has not been updated to new versions, so the protocols using Stringprep are stuck at Unicode 3.2 and their specifications need to be updated to support new versions of Unicode. The protocols would like not to be bound to a specific version of Unicode, but rather have better Unicode version agility in the way of IDNA2008. This matters partly because it is usually impossible for an application to require Unicode 3.2: the application gets whatever version of Unicode is available on the host. The protocols require better bidirectional support than Stringprep currently offers. If the protocols are updated to use a new version of Stringprep or another framework, backward compatibility is an important requirement; Stringprep normalization is based on NFKC, profiles may use NFKC, and IDNA2008 mostly uses NFC. And identifiers are passed between protocols: the same username string of code points may be passed between SASL, XMPP, LDAP and EAP, so a common set of rules or classes of strings is preferred over specific rules for each protocol. Without real planning in advance, many Stringprep profiles reuse other profiles, so this goal was accomplished by accident with Stringprep.

The protocols use Stringprep for different kinds of string. XMPP uses a different profile for each part of the Jabber Identifier: a localpart, which is similar to a username and used for authentication; a domainpart, which is a domain name; and a resourcepart, which is less restrictive than the localpart. iSCSI uses a profile for the names of protocol participants, and the iSCSI Qualified Name format contains a reversed DNS domain name. SASL and LDAP use a profile for usernames, and LDAP uses a set of profiles.

The apparent judgement of the attendees was that it would be highly desirable to have a replacement of Stringprep with similar characteristics to IDNA2008, defined so that the protocols could use internationalized strings without a lot of specialized internationalization work, since internationalization expertise is not available in the respective protocols or working groups. The IESG therefore formed the PRECIS working group to undertake the task. The RFC adds a caveat: IDNA2008 may be a poor model for what other protocols ought to do, because it is designed to support an old protocol operating on the scale of the entire Internet, and is intended to be deployed without any change to the base DNS protocol. Other protocols may aim at deployment in more local environments, or may have protocol version negotiation built in.
sections.plainLanguage: The problems the IETF wanted solved were: the character set is frozen at Unicode 3.2, there is not enough support for right-to-left scripts, and every protocol invents its own rules even though they pass usernames to each other. The fix was a shared framework, and the RFC notes that IDNA2008 is a guide but not a perfect model.

sections.title: Comparison: Three Classes of Identifier
sections.content:
Following the identifier comparison taxonomy, it is possible to organize identifiers into three classes in respect of how they may be compared with one another.

Absolute Identifiers are identifiers that can be compared byte-by-byte for equality. Definite Identifiers are identifiers that have a well-defined comparison algorithm on which all parties agree. Indefinite Identifiers are identifiers that have no single comparison algorithm on which all parties agree.

Definite Identifiers include cases like the comparison of Unicode code points in different encodings: they do not match byte for byte, but can all be converted to a single encoding which then does match byte for byte. Indefinite Identifiers are sometimes algorithmically comparable by well-specified subsets of parties.

The three classes of comparison style may have different effects when applied, and it is necessary to evaluate the effects if a comparison results in a false positive or a false negative, especially in terms of the consequences to security and usability. The appendix that classifies the existing Stringprep profiles uses these categories.
sections.plainLanguage: Some identifiers can be compared as raw bytes. Some have a comparison rule everybody agrees on. Some have no agreed rule at all, and the risk of getting it wrong differs in each case, so a replacement has to say which kind it is dealing with.

sections.title: Dealing with Characters
sections.content:
Case folding, case sensitivity and case preservation. In IDNA2003, labels are always mapped to lowercase before the Punycode transformation. In IDNA2008, there is no mapping at all: input is either a valid U-label or it is not. At the same time, uppercase characters are by definition not valid U-labels, because they fall into the Unstable category of RFC 5892. If there are protocols that require case to be preserved, the analogy with IDNA2008 breaks down. Existing protocols are therefore evaluated against three questions: does the protocol use case folding, for all blocks of code points or just for certain subsets; is the system or protocol case-sensitive; and does the system or protocol preserve case.

Stringprep and NFKC. Stringprep profiles may use normalization, and if they do they use NFKC, as most profiles do. It is not clear that NFKC is the right normalization in all cases. The Unicode standard says of the KC and KD forms that it is best to think of them as being like uppercase or lowercase mappings: useful in certain contexts for identifying core meanings, but also performing modifications to the text that may not always be appropriate. In general NFKC is more aggressive about finding matches between code points than NFC, and for things like the spelling of users' names NFKC may not be the best form to use. At the same time, one of the nice things about NFKC is that it deals with the width of characters that are otherwise similar, by canonicalizing half-width to full-width, and this mapping step can be crucial in practice.

Character mapping. There is the question of whether some characters are mapped either to other characters or to nothing during Stringprep. RFC 3454 outlines a number of characters that are mapped to nothing, and also permits Stringprep profiles to define their own mappings.

Prohibited characters. Many protocols have characters that are simply disallowed, for example control characters and special characters such as '@' or '/'. One of the primary changes of IDNA2008 is the way it approaches Unicode code points, using the inclusion-based approach. Because of the default assumption in IDNA2008 that a code point is not allowed, it has more than one class of allowed code point, unlike IDNA2003. Some code points are disallowed outright and some are allowed only in certain contexts. The reasons for the context-dependent rules have to do with the way some characters are used: the ZERO WIDTH JOINER and ZERO WIDTH NON-JOINER, U+200D and U+200C, are allowed with contextual rules because they are required in some circumstances, yet are considered punctuation by Unicode and would therefore be disallowed under the usual IDNA2008 derivation rules. The goal of IDNA2008 is to provide the widest repertoire of code points possible and consistent with the traditional DNS rule that names contain only letters, digits and hyphens, trusting the operators of individual zones to make sensible and usually more restrictive policies for their zones.

Internal structure, delimiters and special characters. IDNA2008 has a special problem with delimiters, because the delimiter character in the DNS wire format is not really part of the data: labels carry an indicator of their length, and the FULL STOP, U+002E, is used only to break up the labels in the presentation format. Because that separator does not travel with the wire format of the domain name, there is no way to encode a different, internationalized separator in IDNA2008. Other protocols may include characters with similar special meaning. Common ones are FULL STOP, COMMERCIAL AT, HYPHEN-MINUS, SOLIDUS and LOW LINE. The mere inclusion of such a character is not enough for a protocol to be considered similar to another using the same character; the handling of the character must be taken into consideration as well. Whether it is valuable to map to or from these special characters is an important issue: in some locales the analogue to FULL STOP is some other character and users may expect to substitute their normal stop, while there are predictability arguments in favour of treating identifiers containing FULL STOP just as they are treated under IDNA2008.

Restrictions because of glyph similarity. Homoglyphs are similarly or identically rendered glyphs of different code points. For DNS names, homoglyphs may enable phishing. If a protocol requires some visual comparison by end users, the issue of homoglyphs is to be considered. IDNA2008 does not have a mechanism to deal with them, trusting DNS zone operators to enact sensible policies for the subset of Unicode they wish to support, and a similar split between policy and protocol may not be desirable in every protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The hard parts are the characters that carry meaning in one protocol and not another: letters that differ only in case, characters that look alike but are different code points, separators such as the dot or the at sign, and characters that are allowed only in some contexts. A replacement has to decide about each of these, and the RFC walks through what IDNA2008 decided and why that may not transfer.

sections.title: Considerations for a Stringprep Replacement
sections.content:
The RFC's guidance is that a Stringprep replacement should be defined, and that it should take an approach similar to IDNA2008, for example by using properties of code points instead of whitelisting code points, because that enables better Unicode agility. Protocols share similar characteristics of strings, so defining internationalization preparation algorithms for the smallest set of string classes may be sufficient for most cases, providing coherence among a set of related protocols or protocols where identifiers are exchanged. The sets of string classes need to be evaluated according to the considerations in Section 5. It is reasonable to limit scope to Unicode code points and rule the mapping of data from other character encodings outside the scope of this effort. The replacement ought at least to provide guidance to applications on how to handle protocol incompatibilities resulting from changes to Unicode; in an ideal world the replacement would handle the changes automatically, but that appears to require magic and cannot be expected. Compatibility within each protocol between a Stringprep-based technique and its replacement has to be considered very carefully.

Existing deployments already depend on Stringprep profiles, so a replacement must consider the effects of any new strategy on existing deployments. Some characters were acceptable in IDNA labels under IDNA2003 but are not protocol-valid under IDNA2008, and the reverse is also true. Disagreement about what to do during the transition has resulted in different approaches to mapping, and different implementers may make different decisions about what to do in such cases, which could have interoperability effects. It is necessary to trade better support for different linguistic environments against the potential side effects of backward incompatibility.

The RFC adds two related points about where the data comes from and where it goes. Some protocol elements are provided by users and others are not; those that are not may presumably be subject to greater restrictions, while those users provide likely need to permit the broadest range of code points. On the output side, only some protocol elements are intended to be consumed directly by users, and different environments present different challenges: an element only ever delivered as part of a vCard remains in machine-readable format, so the problem of visual confusion is not a great one, but an element published on a business card or on the side of a bus is a different matter.

There is also a question of Unicode-incompatible changes. IDNA2008 derives the validity of a code point by using the properties of each code point, and this approach depends critically on the idea that code points, once valid for a protocol profile, will not later be made invalid. That is not a guarantee currently provided by Unicode: properties of code points may change between versions of Unicode, and rarely such a change could cause a given code point to become invalid under a protocol profile even though the code point was valid with an earlier version of Unicode. This is not merely a theoretical possibility, because it has occurred, as described in RFC 6452. A replacement that intends to be Unicode version agnostic therefore needs a mechanism to address such cases.
sections.plainLanguage: The guidance for the replacement is to follow IDNA2008's lead in deriving the rules from Unicode properties rather than from a hand-written list, to cover as few string classes as possible, and to be honest about the fact that a Unicode update can invalidate a character that used to be allowed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document merely states what problems are to be solved and does not define a protocol. There are undoubtedly security implications of the particular results that will come from the work to be completed. The Stringprep Security Considerations of RFC 3454 apply, and the RFC points to the analysis in the subsections of its appendix, where each existing Stringprep profile is evaluated.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not define a protocol, so it does not define a protocol's security. It says the security analysis of the original Stringprep still applies, and points to the per-profile analysis in the appendix.

viz.caption: THE CHARACTER QUESTIONS A REPLACEMENT MUST ANSWER

items.title: Case
items.text: Fold case, be case-sensitive, or preserve it? Each protocol answers differently.

items.title: Normalization
items.text: NFKC finds more matches between code points than NFC, but changes the text more.

items.title: Character mapping
items.text: Some characters are mapped to other characters, or to nothing at all.

items.title: Prohibited characters
items.text: Control characters and characters like '@' or '/' are disallowed outright in many protocols.

items.title: Delimiters
items.text: Characters such as FULL STOP, COMMERCIAL AT, SOLIDUS and LOW LINE carry meaning in some protocols.

items.title: Glyph similarity
items.text: Look-alike characters from different code points can be used for phishing.
